rmt-2010-power-01a.prompt:
*Setup.* A *graph* is a collection of points (vertices) joined by line segments (edges). All graphs here are simple (two vertices are joined by at most one edge) and connected. An *edge $n$-colouring* of a graph assigns one of $n$ colours to each edge. $K_n$ is the *complete graph* on $n$ vertices (any two vertices are joined by an edge). A *monochromatic $K_k$* is a set of $k$ vertices all of whose joining edges have the same colour.

Draw a simple connected graph with $8$ vertices and $7$ edges, and $3$-colour its edges.
rmt-2010-power-01a.answer: For example the path $v_1v_2\cdots v_8$ with edges coloured red, blue, green, red, blue, green, red.

rmt-2010-power-01b.prompt:
*Setup.* A *graph* is a collection of points (vertices) joined by line segments (edges). All graphs here are simple (two vertices are joined by at most one edge) and connected. An *edge $n$-colouring* of a graph assigns one of $n$ colours to each edge. $K_n$ is the *complete graph* on $n$ vertices (any two vertices are joined by an edge). A *monochromatic $K_k$* is a set of $k$ vertices all of whose joining edges have the same colour.

Draw a complete graph on $5$ vertices, and $2$-colour its edges so that it does not contain a red triangle or a blue triangle ($3$ vertices, the edges between which are all red or all blue). (In other words: colour $K_5$ so that it has no monochromatic $K_3$.)
rmt-2010-power-01b.answer: Pentagon sides blue, the five diagonals red.

rmt-2010-power-02.prompt:
*Setup.* A *graph* is a collection of points (vertices) joined by line segments (edges). All graphs here are simple (two vertices are joined by at most one edge) and connected. An *edge $n$-colouring* of a graph assigns one of $n$ colours to each edge. $K_n$ is the *complete graph* on $n$ vertices (any two vertices are joined by an edge). A *monochromatic $K_k$* is a set of $k$ vertices all of whose joining edges have the same colour.

Show that no matter how you $2$-colour the edges of $K_6$, it will contain a monochromatic $K_3$. (Hint: think about all the edges coming from one vertex.)
rmt-2010-power-02.answer: Every red/blue colouring of $K_6$ has a monochromatic triangle (pigeonhole on the $5$ edges at a vertex).

rmt-2010-power-03a.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(k,j)$ is the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_N$ contains a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_j$. We write $R(k)=R(k,k)$ (the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of $K_N$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$); $K_n$ is the complete graph on $n$ vertices.

Show that $R(3,4)>8$ by exhibiting a $2$-colouring of the edges of $K_8$ with no red $K_3$ and no blue $K_4$.
rmt-2010-power-03a.answer: Label the vertices $0,\dots,7$ (mod $8$). Colour $ij$ red if $i-j\equiv\pm1$ or $4\pmod8$, blue otherwise (differences $\pm2,\pm3$).

rmt-2010-power-03b.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(k,j)$ is the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_N$ contains a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_j$. We write $R(k)=R(k,k)$ (the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of $K_N$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$); $K_n$ is the complete graph on $n$ vertices.

Show that $R(4,3)=9$. (Hint: use Problem 2.)
rmt-2010-power-03b.answer: Every colouring of $K_9$ has a red $K_4$ or a blue triangle (degree counting), and $K_8$ has a colouring with neither.

rmt-2010-power-04a.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(k,j)$ is the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_N$ contains a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_j$. We write $R(k)=R(k,k)$ (the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of $K_N$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$); $K_n$ is the complete graph on $n$ vertices.

Show that $R(n,m)\le R(n,m-1)+R(n-1,m)$ (for $n,m\ge3$, assuming the numbers on the right exist, which is shown in part (b)). (Hint: see the hint to Problem 2.)
rmt-2010-power-04a.answer: Pick a vertex in $K_N$, $N=R(n,m-1)+R(n-1,m)$; it has $N-1$ edges, so at least $R(n-1,m)$ red or at least $R(n,m-1)$ blue; apply the definition inside the neighbourhood.

rmt-2010-power-04b.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(k,j)$ is the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_N$ contains a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_j$. We write $R(k)=R(k,k)$ (the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of $K_N$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$); $K_n$ is the complete graph on $n$ vertices.

Conclude that $R(n,m)$ is well defined, that is, that it exists for every $n$ and every $m$ (with $n,m\ge2$).
rmt-2010-power-04b.answer: Induction on $n+m$ using $R(2,m)=m$, $R(n,2)=n$ and the inequality of part (a).

rmt-2010-power-05a.prompt:
*Setup.* Colour the edges of the complete graph on $n^2$ points laid out in an $n\times n$ grid as follows: the edge $(u,v)$ is blue if $u$ and $v$ are in the same row, and red otherwise.

Show that any $K_{n+1}$ in this graph contains at least one red edge and at least one blue edge.
rmt-2010-power-05a.answer: By pigeonhole two of $n+1$ points share a row (blue edge); a row has only $n$ points, so not all are in one row (red edge).

rmt-2010-power-05b.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(k,j)$ is the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_N$ contains a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_j$. We write $R(k)=R(k,k)$ (the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of $K_N$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$); $K_n$ is the complete graph on $n$ vertices.

Colour the edges of the complete graph on $n^2$ points laid out in an $n\times n$ grid as follows: the edge $(u,v)$ is blue if $u$ and $v$ are in the same row, and red otherwise. Use this (and the fact that any $K_{n+1}$ in it has both a red and a blue edge) to conclude that $R(n+1,n+1)>n^2$.
rmt-2010-power-05b.answer: The grid colouring of $K_{n^2}$ has no monochromatic $K_{n+1}$, so $R(n+1,n+1)>n^2$.

rmt-2010-power-06a.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(k,j)$ is the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_N$ contains a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_j$. We write $R(k)=R(k,k)$ (the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of $K_N$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$); $K_n$ is the complete graph on $n$ vertices.

Show that if the edges of $K_m$ are coloured red or blue randomly with equal probability (i.e. by flipping a coin for each edge), then the probability that it contains a monochromatic $K_n$ is at most $\binom mn\cdot2^{1-\binom n2}$.
rmt-2010-power-06a.answer: Union bound: each of the $\binom mn$ sets of $n$ vertices is monochromatic with probability $2\cdot2^{-\binom n2}$.

rmt-2010-power-06b.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(k,j)$ is the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_N$ contains a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_j$. We write $R(k)=R(k,k)$ (the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of $K_N$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$); $K_n$ is the complete graph on $n$ vertices.

Show that if $\binom mn<2^{\binom n2-1}$, then the probability in the previous problem (that a random red/blue colouring of $K_m$ contains a monochromatic $K_n$) is less than $1$.
rmt-2010-power-06b.answer: The bound $\binom mn2^{1-\binom n2}$ is then less than $1$.

rmt-2010-power-06c.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(k,j)$ is the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_N$ contains a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_j$. We write $R(k)=R(k,k)$ (the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of $K_N$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$); $K_n$ is the complete graph on $n$ vertices.

Using the fact that $\binom mn<m^n$, show that if $m=2^{\frac n2-\frac1n-\frac12}$ then $\binom mn<2^{\binom n2-1}$, and conclude that $R(n,n)>2^{\frac n2-\frac1n-\frac12}$. (Take $n\ge3$.)
rmt-2010-power-06c.answer: $m^n=2^{\binom n2-1}$, so $\binom mn<2^{\binom n2-1}$; hence some colouring of $K_{\lfloor m\rfloor}$ has no monochromatic $K_n$ and $R(n,n)>m$.

rmt-2010-power-07.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(k,j)$ is the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of $K_N$ contains a red $K_k$ or a blue $K_j$. We write $R(k)=R(k,k)$ (the least $N$ such that every red/blue colouring of $K_N$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$); $K_n$ is the complete graph on $n$ vertices.

Prove the complementary upper bound $R(n,n)\le4^n$.
rmt-2010-power-07.answer: Repeatedly pick a vertex and keep the majority-colour neighbourhood; the first $2n$ chosen vertices carry colour flags, and $n$ of them have the same flag.

rmt-2010-power-08.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(n_1,\dots,n_k)$ is the least $m$ such that whenever the edges of $K_m$ are coloured with $k$ colours $c_1,\dots,c_k$, there is some $i$ and a $K_{n_i}$ all of whose edges have colour $c_i$. Here $K_m$ is the complete graph on $m$ vertices.

Prove that $R(3,3,3)\le17$.
rmt-2010-power-08.answer: At a vertex of $K_{17}$ some colour appears on at least $6$ of its $16$ edges; the $K_6$ on the other ends has a triangle in that colour or in the other two colours (by $R(3,3)=6$).

rmt-2010-power-09.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(n_1,\dots,n_k)$ is the least $m$ such that whenever the edges of $K_m$ are coloured with $k$ colours $c_1,\dots,c_k$, there is some $i$ and a $K_{n_i}$ all of whose edges have colour $c_i$. Here $K_m$ is the complete graph on $m$ vertices.

Show that $R(n_1,\dots,n_k)\le R\big(n_1,n_2,\dots,n_{k-2},R(n_k,n_{k-1})\big)$ for $k\ge3$. (This gives the existence of $R(n_1,\dots,n_k)$ for all $n_1,\dots,n_k$.)
rmt-2010-power-09.answer: Merge the last two colours; a monochromatic $K_{R(n_{k-1},n_k)}$ in the merged colour contains a $K_{n_{k-1}}$ of colour $k-1$ or a $K_{n_k}$ of colour $k$.

rmt-2010-power-10a.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(n_1,\dots,n_k)$ is the least $m$ such that whenever the edges of $K_m$ are coloured with $k$ colours $c_1,\dots,c_k$, there is some $i$ and a $K_{n_i}$ all of whose edges have colour $c_i$. Here $K_m$ is the complete graph on $m$ vertices.

Let $R_r=R(3,\dots,3)$ with $r$ threes (so $r$ colours and monochromatic triangles). Prove that $R_r\le3\cdot r!$.
rmt-2010-power-10a.answer: Induction on $r$: at a vertex of $K_{3\cdot r!}$ some colour has at least $3(r-1)!$ edges; the neighbourhood has a triangle in that colour or is $(r-1)$-coloured.

rmt-2010-power-10b.prompt:
*Setup.* $R(n_1,\dots,n_k)$ is the least $m$ such that whenever the edges of $K_m$ are coloured with $k$ colours $c_1,\dots,c_k$, there is some $i$ and a $K_{n_i}$ all of whose edges have colour $c_i$. Here $K_m$ is the complete graph on $m$ vertices.

Let $R_r=R(3,\dots,3)$ with $r$ threes. Prove that $R_r>2^r$.
rmt-2010-power-10b.answer: Build, by induction, an $r$-colouring of $K_{2^r}$ with no monochromatic triangle by doubling and joining the two copies with a new colour.

rmt-2010-power-11.prompt:
*Setup.* Let $K_{\mathbb N}=(V,E)$ with $V=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$ and $E=\{(i,j):i,j\in V,\ i<j\}$; this is in some sense an infinite complete graph.

Show that if every edge is coloured red or blue, there is some infinite subset $V'$ of $V$ such that all of the edges between points of $V'$ are the same colour.
rmt-2010-power-11.answer: Repeatedly pick the least vertex and keep an infinite same-colour neighbourhood; infinitely many of the picked vertices carry the same colour flag.
